A palaeomagnetic and 40Ar/39Ar study of mafic dykes in southern
Sweden: A new Early Neoproterozoic key-pole for the Baltic Shield
and implications for Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops
Sten-Åke Elminga,∗, Sergei A. Pisarevskyb,c, Paul Layerd, Göran Bylunde
aDepartment of Civil, Environmental and Natural Resources Engineering, Luleå University of Technology, SE-07187 Luleå, Sweden
bAustralian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Core to Crust Fluid Systems (CCFS) and the Institute for Geoscience Research (TIGeR),
Department of Applied Geology, Curtain University, GPO Box U1987, Perth, WA 6845, Australia
cSchool of Earth and Environment, University of Western Australia, 35 Stirling Highway, Crawley, WA 6009, Australia
dGeophysical Institute, University of Alaska Fairbanks, AK, USA
eDepartment of Geology, GeoBiosphere Science Centre, Lund University, Sölvegatan 12, SE-22362 Lund, Sweden
a r t i c l e i n f o

Available online 25 December 2013

a

Palaeogeography
Baltica
b s t r a c t
We present the results of palaeomagnetic and40Ar/39Ar studies of the Proterozoic mafic dykes in the
Norrköping and Falun areas of the southern Sweden. The primary remanence of two 939 ± 3 Ma dykes is
supported by the rigorous baked contact test. The remanence direction of two other dykes, one of which
was previously U–Pb dated at 946 ± 1 Ma is close to the reverse direction of 939 Ma dykes. Using these
results together with previously published 935 ± 5 Ma palaeomagnetic data from the Göteborg-Slussen
mafic dykes and some dykes from the Falun area we calculated the mean 946–935 Ma palaeopole for
Baltica (0.9◦S, 240.7◦E, A95= 6.7), which can be qualified as the key pole. Using this pole together with
other date we conclude that the Grenville and Sveconorwegian loops of Laurentian and Baltican Apparent
Polar Wander Paths are temporary displaced by 100–150 m.y. We propose new palaeogeographic recons-
tructions of Baltica and Laurentia at ca. 940 Ma and ca. 850 Ma. We also present two new Mesoproterozoic
non-key poles from 1410 Ma and 1595 Ma dykes.
© 2014 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction
Assembly of continents into a late Precambrian superconti-
nent, Rodinia, has been suggested in a number of studies (e.g.
McMenamin and McMenamin, 1990; Dalziel, 1991, 1997; Hoffman,
1991). Models of Rodinia are mostly based on ca. 1350–1000 Ma
orogenic belts, tectonic links between mobile belts across the cra-
tonic margins, global analyses of the balance of Neoproterozoic
and Early Palaeozoic continental margins and some palaeomag-
netic data. Early Neoproterozoic tectonic reconstructions suggest
a connection between Baltica and Laurentia (e.g. Hoffman, 1991;
Dalziel, 1991, 1997; Weil et al., 1998; Dalziel et al., 2000; Pisarevsky
et al., 2003; Li et al., 2008) in Rodinia. Since palaeomagnetism
is the only tool for reconstructing the latitudinal position and
orientation of cratons it plays an important role for these recons-
tructions. However, reliable palaeomagnetic data are sparse (e.g.
Buchan et al., 2001) and more “key” palaeomagnetic poles, i.e. well
dated poles that fulfill criteria for original magnetization, etc. (Van
∗
Corresponding author. Tel.: +46 920 491392; fax: +46 920491697.
E-mail address: sten-ake.elming@ltu.se (S.-Å.
der
Elming).
Voo, 1990; Buchan et al., 2000) are needed for testing the
palaeogeographic reconstructions. Due to the often high contents
of magnetite, fast cooling and thereby small magnetic grain sizes
and stable remanent magnetizations, mafic dykes are often excel-
lent recorders of the Earth magnetic field. Palaeomagnetic data
from mafic dykes forms a significant part in the palaeomagnetic
databases (e.g. McElhinny and Lock, 1996; Pesonen et al., 2003;
Pisarevsky, 2005).
In southern Sweden Early Neoproterozoic dyke swarms are
widespread and have been the target for a large number of
palaeomagnetic studies (e.g. Poorter, 1975; Patchett and Bylund,
1977; Bylund, 1985, 1992; Bylund and Elming, 1992; Bylund and
Pisarevsky, 2002; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 1998, 2006). Most of these
studies are from dolerite dykes in the Protogine Zone (PZ; Fig. 1)
that defines a metamorphic boundary that separates the Southwest
Scandinavian province in the west from the Transscandinavian
Igneous Belt (TIB; Patchett et al., 1987) and the Southern Sve-
cofennian subprovince (SSv) in the east (e.g. Gaál and Gorbatschev,
1987). The TIB and the Southwest Scandinavian province formed
by crystal growth of the Baltic Shield with a westward younging
during the TIB (ca. 1850–1670; Gorbatschev, 2004) and the Goth-
ian period (1700–1550 Ma) (e.g. Åhäll and Larson, 2000; Andersen
0301-9268/$ – see front matter © 2014 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.precamres.2013.12.007

### page_2
S.-Å. Elming et al. / Precambrian Research 244 (2014) 192–206 193
Fig. 1. The geology of the south-western part of the Fennoscandian Shield (a). The inlet in figure (a) marks the area where this study was concentrated on.
et al., 2004, Högdahl et al., 2004). From the late Palaeoproterozoic
time the continental margin of a suggested continuous Laurentia-
Baltica was the location of long lived subduction and terranes’
accretion (e.g. Åhäll et al., 2000; Karlström et al., 2001; Andersen
et al., 2004; Bingen et al., 2008; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 2010).
The Sveconorwegian (in Laurentia Grenvillian; ca. 1150–900 Ma)
continent-continent collision resulted in deformation and meta-
morphism of the Gothian orogen in Southwestern Sweden (e.g.
Åhäll and Gower, 1997). The event resulted in a major deformation
zone, the Mylonite Zone (Fig. 1; e.g. Gorbatschev, 1980), a zone that
has been active during both Sveconorwegian thrusting and subse-
quent phases of exhumation (e.g. Stephens et al., 1996; Berglund,
1997).40Ar/39Ar hornblende ages from the Mylonite Zone indicate
deformations as late as ca. 915 Ma ago (Page et al., 1996), while ca.
40–70 km away from the Mylonite Zone two Sveconorwegian ages
were identified, at 934–931 Ma and 1007–960 Ma, the younger ages
suggested to be related to orogenic uplift. Deformation up to 40 km
east of the Protogine Zone has been demonstrated from structural
mapping (Wahlgren et al., 1994). Palaeomagnetic data older than
ca. 900 Ma from southwestern Sweden should therefore be used
with caution, since they may have been subjects to metamorphic
overprints or tectonically disturbed and therefore not necessarily
representing the Baltic Shield as a whole.
Palaeomagnetic results from 935 ± 3 Ma mafic dykes (Göteborg-
Slussen dykes; Fig. 1) in the Southwestern Scandinavian province,
west of the Mylonite Zone, were presented by Pisarevsky and
Bylund (2006). The data are of good quality, however, no full field
test demonstrating an original magnetization was presented. Here
we will present a new ca. 935 Ma-highly reliable pole for the Baltic
Shield. This is based on new palaeomagnetic data fulfilling field
test of primary magnetization and 40Ar/39Ar age determinations
from mafic dykes in the eastern part of the Southern Svecofen-
nian subprovince. This pole is compared and combined with the
palaeomagnetic data from the 935 Ma dykes in the Southwest
Scandinavian province and 946 Ma dykes from Dalarna. The
combined
new
palaeomagnetic pole forms an important input to the
discussion of the shape and timing of the Sveconorwegian Appar-
ent Polar Wander Path (APWP) loop (e.g. Patchett and Bylund, 1977;
Elming et al., 1993), which is similar in shape to the Grenville Loop
in the Laurentia APWP (e.g. Hyodo and Dunlop, 1993; Weil et al.,
1998) and has been a basis for palaeogeographic reconstruction of
Baltica vs. Laurentia at 935 Ma.
2. Geology, sampling and laboratory technique
Mafic dykes in the southeastern part of the Southern Svecofen-
nian subprovince (Figs. 1 and 2) comprise several dyke swarms,
Fig. 2. Basic dykes in southern central Sweden (modified from Risku-Norja, 1992).
Sampling localities for this study are marked by filled circles.

### page_3
194 S.-Å. Elming et al. / Precambrian Research 244 (2014) 192–206
Fig. 3. The crossing dykes at site 1. The location of the collected samples for the palaeomagnetic analyses are marked by black dots and those also used for40Ar/39Ar whole
rock dating are marked by a white cross in the black dot. Close to the sample 88 in dyke O1 a number of samples (152–156) have been collected close to each other at
increasing distance from the younger dyke. In dyke O2 a fragment of the host rock is included and marked by the thin black line.
predominantly trending in E–W directions, however, NW–SE, N–S
and a few NE–SW trending dykes are also observed (Risku-Norja,
1992). The dykes intrude gneissic and granitic rocks that were
formed during the Svecofennian orogeny at 1.9–1.8 Ga ago. In the
gneisses there are often amphibolite layers that have been inter-
preted as intrusive sills from a late stage of the orogeny (Wikström,
1975). There are two major groups of 1.9–1.8 Ga intrusive rocks, a
synorogenic suite of granitic to ultrabasic composition and a sero-
rogenic suite with mainly migmatite gneisses. The rocks have been
deformed and sometimes fractured.
The dykes are of tholeiitic to alkaline composition (Risku-Norja,
1992) and they were intruded after the cratonization following the
Svecofennian orogeny, thus distinctly different from intraorogenic
Svecofennian dykes also found in the region. Importantly the stud-
ied dykes are located relatively far from (>100 km), and to the east
of the Protogine Zone and it is unlikely that they were influenced
by late Sveconorwegian overprint. Trace elements data suggest that
the dykes originate from a mantle source (Risku-Norja, 1992). E–W
trending dykes, the Breven-Hällefors dykes (Bylund, 1985), have
been dated at ca. 1595 ± 3 Ma (U–Pb, baddeleyite; Söderlund et al.,
2005; Rejmyre, Fig. 2) and the N–S trending dykes probably belong
to the subparallel Blekinge Dalarna Dolerites (BDD), which
been
have
dated in the range 978–946 Ma (U–Pb baddeleyite; Söderlund
et al., 2005). Apart from the Breven-Hällefors dykes no ages have
been reported for dykes in the area of this study (Fig. 2).
In this study 97 samples were collected from 8 mafic dykes
(Figs. 1 and 2; localities 1–5) in the southeastern part of the South-
ern Svecofennian subprovince and from one dyke (Falun, locality
6; Fig. 1) north of this area. In one locality (locality 1; Fig. 3)
samples were collected from two NE (N38◦E) trending dykes (Y1
and Y2) that cut two NW (N53◦W) trending dykes (O1 and O2),
which formed an excellent opportunity for baked contact tests. The
younger Y1 and Y2 dykes are subvertical, while the O1 and O2 dip
ca. 48◦to the SW. Chilled margins are observed in both generations
of dykes in the contact to the gneiss and in for the younger dykes
also in contact to the older dyke. The samples were collected from
various parts of the dykes and for the baked contact tests in the
older dykes at increasing distances from the younger dykes.
Two other dykes, trending NW (localities 2 and 3, N50–60◦W),
were sampled to the west of locality 1, at a distance of 14 km
and 2 km, respectively (Fig. 2). Both dykes are ca. 1 m wide and
subvertical. The dykes at sites 4 (Rejmyre) and 5 (Hällefors) are
E–W trending and belong to the Breven-Hällefors dyke system. The
Rejmyre dyke is ca. 15 m wide and located ca. 40 km northwest of

the locality 1. The rock at locality 5 forms a part the ca. 1 km wide
Hällefors dolerite dyke and it is located ca. 60 km north–north–east
of locality 1. Both dykes were sampled from their central parts.
The last dyke included in this study (Falun, locality 6, Fig. 1) is
situated north of the area described by Risku-Norja (1992). This
dyke belongs to the 978–946 Ma old Blekinge Dalarna dolerite
(BDD) dyke swarm (Solymon et al., 1992; Söderlund et al., 2005). In
Dalarna different dykes in this swarm has previously been sampled
for palaeomagnetic studies by Patchett and Bylund (1977), Bylund
(1985) and Bylund and Elming (1992). Patchett and Bylund (1977)
collected 10 samples at different locations along the same dyke as
in locality 6 and here we collected 9 samples in a locality where that
dyke has been dated at 945.7 ± 1.2 Ma (–-Pb baddeleyite; Söderlund
et al., 2005).
A portable rock coring drill was used for the sampling and the
samples were oriented with sun and magnetic compasses.
The intensity and direction of remanent magnetization was
measured with a SQUID (2G-DC) magnetometer and the speci-
mens were AF-demagnetized in steps of 5 mT up to 30 mT and in
10 mT steps up to 120 mT. Thermal demagnetizations were per-
formed using a Schonstedt (TDS1) oven at intervals of 50◦C up to
500◦C and 10–30◦C for higher temperatures. The remanence vec-
tors were defined by least square fit of vectors in 3-D space (Torsvik,
1986; Torsvik et al., 1996) and by principle component analyses
(Kirschvink, 1980). The magnetic susceptibility was measured on
crushed specimens during heating and cooling using a  appabridge
(KLY-3 and CS-3, AGICO).
Specimens from the palaeomagnetic samples were also sub-
mitted for 40Ar/39Ar whole rock dating at the Geochronology
laboratory at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. The cores were
crushed, washed and sieved to obtain small (∼0.5 mm) whole-
rock chips for dating. The monitor mineral MMhb-1 (Samson and
Alexander, 1987) with an age of 513.9 Ma (Lanphere and Dalrymple,
2000) was used to monitor neutron flux (and calculate the irradi-
ation parameter, J). The samples and standards were wrapped in
aluminum foil and loaded into aluminum cans of 2.5 cm diame-
ter and 6 cm height. The samples were irradiated in position 5c of
the uranium enriched research reactor of McMaster University in
Hamilton, Ontario, Canada for 20 MW-h.
Upon their return from the reactor, the sample and monitors
were loaded into 2 mm diameter holes in a copper tray that was
then loaded in a ultra-high vacuum extraction line. The monitors
were fused, and samples heated in a step-wise manner, using a 6-
W argon-ion laser following the technique described in York et
(1981),
al.
Layer et al. (1987) and Layer (2000). Argon purification was
achieved using a liquid nitrogen cold trap and a SAES Zr–Al getter at
400◦C. The samples were analyzed in a VG-3600 mass spectrom-
eter at the Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska Fairbanks.
The argon isotopes measured were corrected for system blank and
mass discrimination, as well as calcium, potassium and chlorine
interference reactions following procedures outlined in McDougall
and Harrison (1999). System blanks generally were 2 × 10−16mol
40Ar and 2 × 10−18mol36Ar, which are 10–50 times smaller than
fraction volumes. Mass discrimination was monitored by running
both calibrated air shots and a zero-age glass sample. These mea-
surements were made on a weekly to monthly basis to check for
changes in mass discrimination. Plateau ages (P in Table 1) were
based on the criteria of three or more contiguous fractions (with
a roughly constant Ca/K ratio) accounting for more than 50% gas
release, having a Mean Square Weighted Deviation (MSWD) less
than 2.5. For samples that show “plateau-like” segments, but not
meet the criteria, a weighted average age of the plateau-like steps
is calculated (W in Table 1). Some samples were run twice to check
for reproducibility. A summary of all the40Ar/39Ar results is given
in Table 1, with all ages quoted to the ±1 sigma level and calcu-
lated using the constants of Steiger and Jaeger (1977). Integrated
and plateau ages include error in the irradiation parameter (0.5%).
3. 40Ar/39Ar age determinations
Two samples from the “young” dyke Y1 (samples 96, 99; Fig. 3),
three samples from the “old” dyke O2 (samples 158, 160, 162) and
three samples from the contact (sample 93) and hybrid zone in dyke
O2 (samples 88 and 89) were dated.
The age spectra from the samples collected in the dyke Y1 (96
and 99; Fig. 4) exhibit a slight amount of excess argon (anomalous
old ages for the first steps) and do not meet the criteria for plateaus,
but weighed mean ages for more than 45% of gas release are iden-
tical with an average age of 939 ± 3 Ma (Table 1). For sample 99,
7 fractions comprising 64% of gas release form a well-constrained
isochron age of 941 ± 3 Ma (Fig. 4), confirming the weighted mean
age 941 ± 6 Ma.
The samples from the O2 dyke, which were collected at ca.
15 m from the contact to younger dykes, show evidence of excess
argon, especially in the high Ca/K steps. The average age from the
three samples, two plateau ages and one weighted average age, is
1411 ± 9 Ma.

196 S.-Å. Elming et al. / Precambrian Research 244 (2014) 192–206
Fig. 4. 40Ar/39Ar whole rock age data (Table 1) from the dykes at locality 1 (for location of the samples see Fig. 3). The Y (O) denotes dated samples from the young (old) dykes.
Some samples are run twice to check for reproducibility. For dyke Y1 an isochron age (A) was defined, with fraction included in the calculation shown by the small arrows.
This age supports the weighted average age of the dyke (C). Ages from the dyke O1 are determined for samples ca. 15 m away from the young dykes (B) and for samples in
the contact to the dyke Y1, and at 0.95 m and 1.4 m from the contact to Y1(D).
Sample 93 is collected from the baked contact in dyke O1 (Fig. 3)
as part of a transect of samples collected at increasing distances
from the contact to the young dyke Y1. Two runs of this sample
give reproducible results with age spectra that are saddle-shaped,
i.e. older at high and low 39Ar release due to excess argon. The
youngest weighted average age in each saddle is ca. 1173 Ma, which
means the sample was not totally reset by the intrusion of the dyke
Y1, but still retains some of its older argon. The spectra steps up
to an age of ca. 1800 Ma, but a correct age for the dyke is difficult
to estimate from these data. The samples collected at 0.95 m (89)
and 1.4 m (88) from the contact were run twice and with repro-
ducible results. The first part of the spectrum from the sample at
0.95 m is characterized by argon loss and very anomalous high Ca/K
ratios, perhaps due to plagioclase microinclusions. The second part
of the spectrum has low Ca/K ratios, reflecting the groundmass of
the dyke, and an average age of 1378 ± 12 Ma. This age is about
30 Ma younger than the age of the O2 dyke as determined on sam-
ples outside the hybrid zone. That age difference could reflect either
a different event or a small amount of argon loss due to the young
dyke intrusion. The third part of the spectrum steps up to ages of ca.
1700 Ma and probably reflects excess argon. The spectrum from the
sample 88 is more or less identical to that of 89 and the weighted
average age from two runs is 1399 ± 20 Ma, i.e. similar to the age
of the sample 89. The amount of excess argon in the high temper-
ature release is much lower than that from the samples collected
in the contact to the cutting dyke and at 0.95 m from the contact,
suggesting a relationship between excess argon and distance from
the dyke

Palaeomagnetic results
4.1. Locality 1, crossing dykes
Samples were collected from the young dykes, the baked con-
tacts and at increasing distance from the contact in the older dykes
(O1 and O2). The characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) in
the Y1 and Y2 dykes is isolated in a high coercivity (demagnetiz-
ing fields 25–120 mT) and medium to high unblocking temperature
(400–580◦C; Fig. 5a) range and the mean directions are not sig-
nificantly different (Y1: decl. = 311.2◦, incl. = −43.3◦, ˛ =
95
5.7◦and
Y2: decl. = 313.3◦, incl. = −40.7◦, ˛ =
95
7.4◦; Table 2; Fig. 7a). The
remanent magnetization in samples from the baked older dykes,
within ca. 0.3 m from the contact, is isolated after treatment in
temperatures between 500 and 580◦C (Fig. 5c). The mean direc-
tion (decl. = 311.5◦, incl. = −45.4◦; Table 2; Fig. 7a) is very well
defined (˛ =
95
3.2◦) and not significantly different from the ChRM
of the cutting dykes Y1 and Y2. In the samples collected in the
hybrid zone (see Elming et al., 2009), at distances of 0.8–1.7 m
from the contact, two components of magnetization were iso-
lated. The first one (in O1 and O2: decl. = 344.3◦, incl. = −22.8◦)
is isolated in the Tub range 300–530◦C, while the second one
(O1, decl. = 173.7◦, incl. = 24.4◦; O2, decl. = 179.9◦, incl. = 10.8◦) is
defined in higher unblocking temperature (500–580◦C) ranges.
Outside the hybrid zone, in intermediate to high unblocking
temperatures (Tub ≥ 450◦C), remanences with shallow negative
to positive inclinations are identified and also traced in very
high coercivities (130–160 mT; Fig. 5b). The mean directions of

Tub and coercivity components inside the hybrid zone. The high
Tub-directions from the hybrid zone (H) and high coercivity and
intermediate to high Tub-direction outside the hybrid zone (U)
are combined for mean calculations (O1a (H + U); decl. = 172.6◦,
incl. = 22.9◦; and O2b (H + U); decl. = 172.8◦, incl. = 19.7◦; Table 2;

and Clegg, 1962), i.e. distinct stable remanence directions in the
cutting dyke, and two remanence components in the hybrid zone,
one of which with a lower Tub similar to the ChRM of the cutting
dyke and another with a higher Tub similar to the host’ ChRM.
Outside the hybrid zone in one of the old dykes (O2) a low Tub
and intermediate to high coercivity component is isolated with
a direction (O2; decl. = 153.8◦, incl. = −29.5◦; Fig. 5b; Table 2) not
identified earlier in these dykes. Possibly there is still a thermal
influence from the young dyke outside the hybrid zone (>1.8 m from
the contact) and this component may be an artifact combination

of
“older” and “younger” components caused by overlapping of
their Tub and coercivity spectra.
4.2. Locality 2
The Borg dyke carries a NRM (Fig. 6a; S2010.02) with a median
destructive field (MDF, Dunlop and Özdemir, 1997) of ca. 15 mT.
Three different components could be isolated, one erased in very
low alternating field intensities (<20 mT) with a direction close to
that of the present Earth field (PEF), a second of intermediate to
high coercivity (decl. = 4.7◦, incl. = 16.2◦) and a third isolated after AF
treatment in field higher than the previous components (>65 mT).
The second component may be an artifact resulting from overlap-
ping coercivity spectra expressed by the gradual change in direction
along a great circle from the low to the highest coercivity direction.
The mean remanence direction of the highest coercivity compo-
nent (decl. = 181.5◦, incl. = 28.9◦, ˛ =
95
14.4◦; Table 2; Fig. 7b) is not

4.3. Locality 3
The coercivity of the NRM carried by the Marbystrand dyke
is rather low with a MDF of 13–20 mT (Fig. 6b; S2011.02). After
removing a soft and poorly defined part of the remanence a sta-
ble component is isolated in AF higher than ca. 30 mT and a
well defined mean ChRM direction is calculated (decl. = 127.5◦,
incl. = 31.1◦, ˛ =
95
3.6◦; Table 2; Fig. 7a). Even though a stable rema-
nence can be defined, the direction of remanence often
along
changes
a great circle during AF demagnetization. Great circle anal-
ysis reveal a direction of intersecting great circles (decl. = 128.7◦,
incl. = 27.8◦) supporting the mean calculated from the stable rema-
nence directions. The mean ChRM direction is antipodal to the
ChRM directions of dykes Y1 and Y2, i.e. the reversal test is positive
with classification C (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990).
4.4. Locality 4
The NRM of the dyke in Rejmyre (1595 ± 3 Ma, Söderlund et al.,
2005), which forms part of the Breven-Hällefors system of dykes,
is of very low coercivity and >90% of the magnetization is lost

in AF higher than 25 mT (Fig. 6c; 174.01). This direction is not very

4.5. Locality 5
The Hällefors dyke carries a remanence with a large portion of
low coercivity (MDF ca. 10 mT; Fig. 6d; B57.97), but also rather well
defined (MAD < 8◦) high coercivity components that form a fairly
well defined site mean (decl. = 21.9◦, incl. = −19.7◦, ˛ =
95
15.3◦).
After changing the polarity of this site mean it is not significantly
different from high coercivity and unblocking temperature compo-
nents of the O1 and O2 dykes at locality 1 and from the site means
in localities 2 and 4 (Fig. 7b).
4.6. Locality 6
The BDD dyke here has been dated at 946 ± 1 Ma (Söderlund
et al., 2005). Well defined ChRM directions (MAD < 5◦) are iden-
tified in this dyke after 40 mT AF demagnetizations (Fig. 6e).
The site mean direction (decl. = 128.7◦, incl. = 37.9◦) is also well
defined (  =
95
3.0◦; Table 2; Fig. 7a) and have a polarity oppo-
site to the directions of the ChRM of the Y1 and Y2 dykes at
locality 1.
5. Origin of magnetization and anisotropy of magnetic
susceptibility
The magnetization in the “young” dykes (Y1 and Y2) at local-
ity 1 is carried by low-titanium titanomagnetite as indicated
from unblocking temperatures (>ca. 530◦C) and susceptibility vs. temperature ( –T) measurements (Curie temperature ca. 550◦C;
Fig. 5a and 8a). This is true also for the baked contact of the “old”

### page_9
200 S.-Å. Elming et al. / Precambrian Research 244 (2014) 192–206
Fig. 8. Magnetic susceptibility during heating and cooling of samples from the Y2
and O2 dykes at site 1.
dyke O1 at the same locality, however, the Curie temperature
indicates a somewhat higher titanium content (Fig. 8b). The pres-
ence of small, but noticeable, Hopkinson peaks in the  –T curves
indicate that the remanence is carried in part by highly stable
single-domain particles. Since single-domain particles carry stable
remanent magnetizations, this gives an additional evidence for a
primary magnetization.
The measurements of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility
(AMS) show a degree of anisotropy of 5–10% for the O1 and O2
dykes, 3–7% for the Y1 and Y2 dykes and less than 10% for the Falun
dyke, which is the usual for igneous rocks with a primary mag-
netic fabric (Hrouda, 1982). The shape of the anisotropy ellipsoid
is expressed by the shape parameter T (Jelinek, 1981), for which
0 < T < 1 express oblate shaped ellipsoid and −1 < T < 0 express a pro-
late ellipsoid. T values are here positive (T = 0.09–0.88), indicating
that the magnetic fabric for the dykes is oblate, i.e. the dykes are
magnetically foliated. We interpret the AMS data as a primary flow
indicator (Knight and Walker, 1988; Tauxe et al., 1998). The AMS
data reveal orientations of the foliation planes of the young dyke
Y1 (strike 29◦E, dip 83◦) that are parallel to the dyke plane. Also for
the O1 and O2 dykes the magnetic foliation planes (strike 217◦E,
dip 46◦) are parallel to the dyke planes, which are thus not ver-
tical but dip ca. 45◦to the southwest. This may suggest that these
older dykes were initially inclined or that they have been tilted after
intrusion.
The Falun dyke is also magnetically foliated, with a subver-
tical foliation plane (dip = 84◦NE) trending 332◦E, i.e. parallel to
the trend of the dyke determined by geological mapping
6.
(SGU,
1964).
Discussion
6.1. New 945–932 Ma high quality pole for Baltica
The new 939 ± 3 Ma palaeomagnetic data from dykes Y1 and
Y2 presented here is supported by rigorous baked contact test.
There are several previously published ca. 970–910 Ma Baltican
palaeopoles, some of them are precisely dated, but there were not
a single one with proven primary ChRM (Table 3). However, the
mean pole from just two dykes should be qualified as represent-
ing a near instantaneous recording of the Earth’s magnetic field,
and is not likely to have averaged palaeo-secular variation (PSV).
To obtain a really valuable ‘key’ pole other palaeomagnetic results
of similar age are needed.
Pisarevsky and Bylund (2006) published a palaeomagnetic study
of the four 935 ± 3 Ma (U–Pb baddeleyite; Hellström et al., 2004)
Göteborg and Slussen dykes carrying bipolar ChRM directions very
similar to that of Y1 and Y2 dykes.
The 946 ± 1 Ma (U–Pb baddeleyite; Söderlund et al., 2005)
Falun dyke carries almost the same ChRM direction (Locality 6;
Plat = −1.7◦, Plon = 242.3◦, A =
95
2.6◦) as reversed Y1 and Y2 direc-
tions. It is also similar to the previous study of the same Falun
dyke by Patchett and Bylund (1977; Plat. = −6.1◦, Plon. = 237.6◦,
A =
95
5.7◦), however somewhat better defined. Considering that
the remanence directions of Patchett and Bylund (1977) were not
defined using vector analysis and the mean direction was calculated
from least scatter in magnetic directions during demagnetization,
which was the best approach at the time, we use the new pole pre-
sented here to represent the Falun dyke (locality 6, Table 2). Bylund
and Elming (1992) and Bylund (1985) studied three dykes (Ander-
sbro, Gällsjön and Ejen) located nearby and trending in the same
direction as the Falun dyke. The ChRM directions are coherent and
also very close to that of the Falun dyke Table 3; Fig. 7), which may
argue for them being part of the same generation of dykes. The
age difference between the Y1/Y2 dykes and BDD Falun dykes is
relatively small (939 ± 3 and 946 ± 1 Ma).
Importantly, the Y1/Y2 dykes in Norrköping area and Falun
dykes are located ca. 90–100 km east of the Protogine zone, i.e.
much further to the east than has been suggested for the limit
of crystal reworking during the Svecororwegian (Wahlgren et al.,
1994). K–Ar ages of biotite from southeast Sweden (Åberg, 1978)
indicate that the K–Ar system started to close at ca. 1.55 Ma and was
completed at ca. 1.40 Ma, i.e. the rocks were not reheated above
ca. 300 ± 50◦C, the closure temperature for K–Ar in biotite. Fis-
sion track studies (Tullborg et al., 1996) of subsidence and uplift
from an area some 150 km south of the present study area, reveal
temperatures of the present surface at 250 ± 50◦C at 820 ± 88 Ma.
This resetting of the fission-track ages was interpreted related to
sedimentary burial and uplift. This means that any tectonic disturb-
ance or palaeomagnetic overprint related to the Sveconorwegian
orogeny is unlikely.
As will be shown later, the drift velocity of Baltica at that
time was apparently low, which makes it reasonable to combine
the Y1/Y2, Göteborg-Slussen and Falun area data and here we
present a mean 946–935 Ma pole, based on 10 different dykes:
Plat. = −0.9◦, Plon. = 240.7◦, A =
95
6.7◦(Table 3). The reversal test of
McFadden and McElhinny (1990) is positive with classification C,
 /  cr= 5.6◦/15.8◦.
The ChRM direction of the Marbystrand dyke (locality 3) is also
very close to the reversed Y1/Y2 direction (Fig. 7a). It is located
only 2 km from them (Fig. 2), but has a significantly different trend,
similar to the Breven-Hällefors swarm. However, the available
palaeomagnetic directions from the latter are significantly differ-
ent (Fig. 7b; Table 3) suggesting that the Marbystrand dyke may
be related to the 939 ± 3 Ma magmatism. A combined pole based
on eleven dykes (Y1, Y2, Marbystrand, Göteborg-Slussen and Falun

area BDD dykes) is calculated (Table 3) and the reversal test is also
positive with classification C,  /  cr= 4.1◦/15.6◦. Both of these two
combined poles (Table 3, entries 11 and 13) have quality factors (Q)
of 7 (Van der Voo, 1990) and fulfill the criteria for a “key” palaeo-
magnetic pole. That is: (1) the rocks are well dated; (2) the number
of samples is sufficient and the statistical demands a fulfilled; (3)
the samples have been adequately demagnetized; (4) field test con-
strain the age of magnetization; (5) there is a structural control and
tectonic coherence with craton involved; (6) there are both nor-
mal and reversed magnetizations; (7) there is no resemblance to
palaeomagnetic poles of younger Neoproterozoic (e.g. Pisarevsky
et al., 2008) or Phanerozoic (e.g. Torsvik et al., 2012) ages.
This combined pole also fulfills the criteria for a key palaeomag-
netic pole used by Buchan et al. (2000), i.e. the age uncertainty is
<±20 Ma, the remanence is properly isolated by AF and/or thermal
demagnetizations, sufficient number of dykes to average out secu-
lar variations, the pole is demonstrated primary through field and
reversal tests and dykes of similar age from a broad geographic area
yield consistent poles.
6.2. New palaeopoles for 1595 ± 3 and 1411 ± 9 Ma
The Hällefors A (entry 37, Table 4; Piper, 1980) and locality 5
(Hällefors) poles most probably are from the same giant dyke. This
dyke has a similar trend as the 1595 ± 3 Ma Rejmyre dyke (local-
ity 4). ChRMs of two dykes are nearly antipodal (Table 2; Fig. 7b)
and the palaeopoles are not significantly different from poles of the
ca. 1570 Ma Kumlinge-Brändö and Föglö Sottunga dykes in Finland
(Fig. 9; Table 4, entries 39–40). Hence we suggest that the Hälle-
fors dyke belongs to the same magmatic event as the ca. 1595 Ma
Rejmyre dyke. These two new VGPs are included to the Table 4
(entries 36 and 38).
Field observations and orientation of magnetic foliation plane
indicate that the O1 and O2 dykes in site 1 are not vertical but
dip ca. 45◦ to the southwest. Since there are no geological evi-
dence for a post- 1411 ± 9 Ma and pre- 939 ± 3 Ma tilting, an initial
inclined emplacement of the dyke is likely. The calculated pole
positions (O1a: Plat. = 19.2◦, Plon. = 204.0◦ and O2a: Plat. = 21.0◦,
Plon. = 203.9◦, Table 2) are not significantly different from the pole
calculated from the dyke at locality 2 (Borg) and a mean ca. 1411 Ma
pole (entry 23 in Table 2; Fig. 9) is calculated from the O1a, O2a
dykes and the Borg dyke (locality 2) poles. This mean pole plots
not so far from the ca. 1450–1470 Ma reference poles (Fig. 9;
Table 4, entries 24–33), and the 10–15◦difference can be explained
by 40–60 m.y. difference in age. Although only three dykes are
included in the mean and secular variations are most probably not
averaged out, this pole adds new data to the gap in reliable Baltica
poles between ca. 1450 and 1270
6.3.
Ma.
Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops and palaeogeographic
implications
There is a strong geological evidence for the close position
of Baltica and Laurentia during almost the whole Neoproterozoic
(e.g. Winchester, 1988; Gee et al., 1994; Fairchild and Hambrey,
1995; Higgins et al., 2001). The match between the two conti-
nents was in part based on the apparent similarity between the
so-called Grenville and Sveconorwegian APWP (Apparent Polar
Wander Path) loops. There were debates about the exact shapes
and the direction of younging of the poles (clockwise vs. anti-
clockwise loops; Fig. 10; e.g. Weil et al., 1998; Hyodo and Dunlop,
1993; Elming et al., 1993; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 1998), but there
was a general agreement about two important features. First,
the “bottoms” of both loops were marked with palaeopoles of
ca. 980–930 Ma (the poles with highest southern latitudes). Sec-
ond, the near-equatorial parts of both loops are populated by ca.
1000–1020 Ma poles and ca. 900–800 Ma poles.
The southern-most part of the Laurentian (Grenville) loop was
constrained by palaeopole from the Haliburton Intrusion A (Buchan
and Dunlop, 1976), with age estimated by authors at 980 ± 10 Ma.
Fig. 9. Mean pole position (23) for the “old” 1411 Ma dykes O1, O2 and Locality 2
(Borg), together with the new 1595 Ma pole of Reymyre (36), both marked by the red
confidence circle, and ca. 1400–1600 Ma reference poles for Baltica (pole numbers
are as in Table 4).

Warnock et al. (2000) restudied this intrusion both geochrono-

estimate of the age of this magnetization is ca. 30–40 m.y. older,
between 1030 and 1000 Ma.
The southernmost part of the Baltica (Sveconorwegian) loop was
constrained by several studies of the ca. 930 Ma Rogaland Igneous
Complex (RIC) and related rocks (e.g. Table 4, entries 10–12). These
poles are in an apparent contradiction with the new key pole,
which is presented in this study, and all of them revealed steep
upwards ChRM directions. Brown and McEnroe (2004) suggested
a significant difference between the time of intrusion and the
age of ChRM, suggesting the latter to be ca. 900 Ma. Walderhaug
et al. (1999) presented a well-dated 848 Ma primary pole from
the Hunnedalen dykes, which was very close to the poles from
the Rogaland complex. Lately Walderhaug et al. (2007) obtained a
869 ± 14 Ma40Ar/39Ar biotite age from a noritic dyke related to RIC
and argued that it represents an uplift/cooling age, which better
represents the age of the remanence in SW Norway. Palaeomag-
netic studies of mostly undated >60 mafic dykes in the Protogine
Zone in southern Sweden revealed that ChRM of all dykes south of
the Ljungby – Alvesta road, i.e. south of the 57◦N latitude, is upward
steep, like the RIC ChRM. Most of dykes north of this line are mag-
netized with more shallow inclinations, similar to the BDD
in
dykes
the Falun area. Pisarevsky and Bylund (1998) also found RIC-like
remanence direction in the ca. 950–930 Ma metamorphic rocks in
southern Sweden west of the Protogine Zone. Such geographically
bound distribution of ChRM directions suggests a regional remag-
netization event. The timing of this remagnetization is probably
constrained by the ca. 870–850 Ma poles of Walderhaug et al. (1998,
2007), but the mechanism is unclear. Page et al. (1996) reported a
detailed40Ar/39Ar study in the Eastern Segment of the Sveconor-
wegian orogen in southern Sweden. They did not find any ages
younger than 915 Ma. Hence the ca. 870–850 Ma remagnetization
event in southern Sweden, if occurred, should have been of a low-
temperature nature. New studies are necessary.
We agree with Walderhaug et al. (1998, 2007) and suggest that
the real age of the southernmost palaeopoles constraining the Sve-
conorwegian loop is likely to be ca. 870–850 Ma. If so, the Grenville
and Sveconorwegian loops are not coeval – their age difference is
ca. 150 Ma (Fig. 11). However, most poles used for the Grenville
loop were from poorly dated metamorphic rocks with uncertain
age of their remanence. Using only well-dated Laurentian poles,
only the older, “downward” part of the Grenville loop is palaeo-
magnetically constrained and there are no reliable Laurentian poles
between 1000 and 790 Ma (Fig. 11; Table 5). On the other hand, Sve-
conorwegian loop is poorly defined between ca. 1100 and 1000 Ma

by just two poles with very imprecise ages (Table 4, entries 18–19),
but better between ca. 960–840 Ma (Fig. 11).
In spite of this incompatibility of the two APWP loops, we still
suggest the integrity of Laurentia and Baltica in the Neoprotero-
zoic as it is shown in Fig. 12. First, there is a geological evidence for
this reconstruction after ca. 1000 Ma (e.g. Li et al., 2008; Pisarevsky
et al., 2008; Cawood et al., 2010 and references therein). In partic-
ular, it is consistent with the existence of the long-lived Meso- to
Neoproterozoic passive continental margin along the eastern and
northeastern edge of Baltica. The eastern Greenland was also a pas-
sive continental margin during most of Neoproterozoic (Li et al.,
2008 and references therein), which is consistent with the recon-
struction in Fig. 12. On the contrary, outcrops of Neoproterozoic
sediments in western Scandinavia are fragmented and generally
interpreted to represent non-marine environments in the middle
of Laurentia-Baltica continent (Fig. 12; e.g. Winchester, 1988). Sec-
ond, the coeval ca. 615 Ma poles from Laurentia and Baltica (Murthy
et al., 1992; Kamo and Gower, 1994; Walderhaug et al., 2007) sup-
port this reconstruction for the Early Ediacaran time and match the
suggested model of the Late Ediacaran opening of the Iapetus ocean
(e.g. Pisarevsky et al., 2008).
Fig. 12 shows the palaeomagnetically permissive reconstruction
of Laurentia and Baltica (the central part of Rodinia) at 940 and
870 Ma. The closeness of ca. 960–920 Ma poles (Table 4; Fig. 10)
suggests little movement of Laurentia – Batica in low latitudes
(Fig. 12a). After ca. 910 Ma there was a quick southward movement

of the two, which resulted in the near-polar position of Baltica at
ca. 870–850 Ma.
7. Conclusions
We obtained the first age determinations for mafic dykes in the
southeastern part of the southern Svecofennian Subprovince.

### page_14
S.-Å. Elming et al. / Precambrian Research 244 (2014) 192–206 205
The palaeomagnetic and geochronological study of the
939 ± 3 Ma mafic dykes near Norrköping, Sweden revealed a pri-
mary remanence supported by a rigorous contact test.
Averaging this and previously published palaeomagnetic results
on coeval mafic dykes in other areas provide a new 946–935 Ma key
pole for Baltica. This primary pole is significantly different from the
palaeopole of the ca. 930 Ma Rogaland Igneous Complex (RIC) and
some coeval mafic and metamorphic rocks in southern Sweden. We
support the previous suggestion of Walderhaug et al. (2007), that
the remanence of RIC-related rocks in southern Norway is signifi-
cantly younger than the time of the igneous event. We also suggest a
low-temperature remagnetization event in southern Sweden after
ca. 900 Ma.
The new 946–935 Ma pole indicates that the distribution of
poles in the “Sveconorwegian loop” was clockwise as has also been
suggested for the Grenville loop of Laurentia.
Palaeogeographic reconstructions demonstrate a slow low lati-
tudinal drift of joint Laurentia – Baltica continents between ca. 960
and 920 Ma and a quick movement towards the polar area by ca.
870–850 Ma.
The two new palaeopoles of ca. 1411 Ma and ca. 1595 Ma added
to the palaeomagnetic database give new constrains to the appar-
ent polar wander of Baltica.
